seal.statement: At the production-defined settled cold-seed checkpoint before the first join, the simulator hosts 45 critical partition groups, 3 replica identities per group and 135 actual Raft-capable replica runtimes, every one of them executing on node-0 and charging the single node-0 busyUntil - and every identity, grouping, placement, peer set and election start comes from the same production owners that create them outside the simulator, never from harness constants. A joining node becomes a member without automatically receiving a replica; a replica appears on a joiner only after the production placement or operation owner authorises one.

text: The production construction authority is traced and every arrow has exactly one owner, measured not assumed. SYSTEM_TABLE_SCHEMAS declares 45 tables, INITIAL_PARTITION_IDS 45 partition ids, and getInitialReplicaIds returns 3 ids for every one of them - 135 replica identities, e.g. tables-p1-r1/r2/r3. SeedPartitionsPhase.phasePartitions builds peerAddresses as nodeId/partition/replicaId using d.getNodeId() for ALL three, which is precisely the seed concentration the live failure needs, and queues each replica with deferElection true. The chain is: SYSTEM_TABLE_SCHEMAS and INITIAL_PARTITION_IDS own which groups exist; getInitialReplicaIds owns the replica policy and identities; SeedPartitionsPhase owns placement and peers; queueBootstrapServiceReplica hands the descriptor to the registration owner, and bootstrap-service-replica-registration-methods.js createPartitionService owns runtime construction; deferElection plus a later phase owns election start. Two facts make adaptation cheaper than feared: PartitionService already defaults dbPath to the in-memory store, so storage needs no new seam, and the simulator's node hosts already supply messageRouter, rebalanceCoordinator, cdcIntegrationService, sqlQueryEngine and systemTableCache. Two facts make it larger than one slice: the phase QUEUES while a separate registration owner CONSTRUCTS, so hosting only the phase would leave the harness constructing - the exact violation - and SeedPartitionsPhase reaches 31 delegate methods, several of them bootstrap-internal bookkeeping such as queueBootstrapServiceReplica, createBootstrapServiceDescriptor, triggerBootstrapReconciler, waitForMessageGroupLeadership and setEpochManager. PartitionService additionally needs transport, messageGroupService and bootstrapReadinessState, none of which the simulator composes today.

Slice A audit: the node-identity singletons are hit in the FIRST seed phase, before anything interesting, and BootstrapService owns the node composition the simulator currently builds in parallel. SeedInfrastructurePhase.phaseInfrastructure - phase one - calls ConfigurationManager.getInstance().initialize({node: {id: nodeId}}) and NodeService.getInstance().initialize({nodeId, nodeAddress}), then reads node identity and address back OUT of NodeService, and later BootstrapService reads NodeService.getInstance().getNodeStats() for heartbeat options. NodeService holds nodeId, nodeAddress, status, a lifecycle state machine, a services map, a messageGroupServices map, heartbeat and stats intervals and startTime as a static single instance. Five virtual nodes in one process would therefore share one production node identity and one node-local service registry, which is precisely the hazard flagged. Surface size: 48 NodeService.getInstance() sites across src, concentrated in bootstrap node-joining (9 + 6 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2), and 69 ConfigurationManager.getInstance() sites spread across transport, rebalancer and query. Second structural fact: BootstrapService initialises this.transport, this.messageRouter, this.cdcIntegrationService, this.systemTableCache, this.rebalanceCoordinator and this.tablePolicyService to null and has its phases CREATE them - phaseInfrastructure builds the message router through MessageRouterSetup.create and sets transport from it. So these are not injectable ports today; hosting the real BootstrapService means it composes the node, and createSimulatedNodeHosts becomes a competing composition of the same objects rather than a set of adapters to hand it.

A0 done and A1b audited. A0: the metered oracle now carries purpose substrate_regression_only, formationCorrespondence false, and names the composition it measured - legacySyntheticFormationComposition, six cohorts keyed from table ids with one LifeRaft per node per group. Its hashes are untouched and the wording is explicit that it is VALID for the sealed legacy substrate composition and NOT authoritative for production-composed formation, so a composition change cannot read as a substrate regression; the correspondence artifact records the same lifecycle and the temporary gates that stand in for an oracle during A1 to D. A1b classification, measured from NodeService.initialize: ConfigurationManager is consulted only as a FALLBACK for node id - options.nodeId wins - plus heartbeat and stats intervals, so it is process-shared configuration rather than runtime identity and does not need per-node instances; LoggingService is process-wide with node identity already in the records; AddressManager holds process-wide nodeAddresses and serviceAddresses conflict Sets and generates an address only when none is supplied, so with explicit addresses it is a shared registry rather than node-local semantics, to be verified rather than assumed; ServiceThreadManager holds a services Map and a pool as a singleton, node-local mutable in principle and reached from exactly one site in src; and NodeService's own services and messageGroupServices Maps are unambiguously node-local mutable state and are the thing that must not be shared. So the demonstrably node-local surface is far smaller than the 48 plus 69 raw site counts: NodeService's own registries first, then ServiceThreadManager if the hosted path reaches it. Proof-cone consumers to migrate first are SeedInfrastructurePhase, message-router-setup.js line 66 which resolves NodeService itself, and control-plane-setup.js lines 488, 596 and 621 which read lifecycle state and node stats.

All four A1 discriminators are measured, and they land exactly on the predicted pattern, which makes A1a small and explicit. A1d-0 GREEN: two NodeService objects constructed directly, never through getInstance, initialised concurrently with no reset, keep distinct nodeId, nodeAddress, lifecycleStateMachine, services Map, messageGroupServices Map and node-local SystemTableCache - and a cache mutation, a service registration and a message-group registration on A are invisible in B. So NodeService's object state is already instance-isolated and the defect is purely how production consumers ACQUIRE the instance. A1d-1 RED: both runtimes hold the same ServiceThreadManager, and it is semantically visible rather than an identity aesthetic - giving A's manager a pool with completed 41 makes B report completed 41 through getNodeStats().threadPool, which production heartbeat and control-plane paths consume as node-local evidence. AddressManager GREEN: the registry is process-wide but decided neither address, because both runtimes supplied their own; with explicit addresses it is observationally inert for this proof cone, so it gets no dependency. A1c RED and it is the driving defect: with the process ConfigurationManager holding a node id belonging to neither runtime, two real SeedInfrastructurePhase runs back to back with no reset leave the SECOND phase carrying node-A's identity and address, because NodeService.getInstance().initialize() returns early once initialised and the phase reads identity back out of the singleton. The hostile configuration value never appeared as either runtime's identity, so no ConfigurationManager consumer in this path treats configuration as runtime identity - which is why 69 config sites do not need migrating. Both defects are asserted as they behave today, named as defects that must invert when the seam lands, so the suite states the truth instead of carrying known-red tests. The resulting A1a shape is: NodeService gains an explicit threadManager dependency defaulting to ServiceThreadManager.getInstance(), and the proof-cone consumers - SeedInfrastructurePhase, MessageRouterSetup, ControlPlaneSetup, BootstrapService stats paths - accept an explicit NodeService defaulting to NodeService.getInstance().

A1a landed with its witnesses flipped in the same change, and it is small exactly as the discriminators predicted. NodeService takes an optional threadManager, defaulting to ServiceThreadManager.getInstance(), and its own shutdown already retires whatever manager it holds so virtual runtimes tear down in isolation without a simulator path. SeedInfrastructurePhase takes options.nodeService defaulting to the singleton and uses that same object for initialize, getNodeId and getNodeAddress, never reacquiring after initialisation. MessageRouterSetup.create takes nodeService and createNodeWebSocketAddressResolver closes over exactly that instance, so the chain stays node runtime to NodeService to node-local cache to router resolution with no cache passed separately. ControlPlaneSetup.create and registerNode each resolve one nodeService and route lifecycle state, node stats and the heartbeat getStats through it rather than three injected values. BootstrapService stores one nodeService for its lifetime and hands the same instance to the phase, which hands it to the router setup. ConfigurationManager, LoggingService, AddressManager and ServiceThreadManager.getInstance itself are untouched, and no ALS, node-id registry or service locator was added. Witnesses: A1c now requires phase A to end as node-A and phase B as node-B with a hostile process configuration id that appears nowhere, and its mutation - the phase reacquiring the singleton - makes B resolve node-A. A1d-1 now requires B to report its own empty pool while A reports completed 41, and its mutation - one shared manager - makes B report 41. The five-runtime closure constructs node-0 to node-4 together with no reset and proves five distinct identities, addresses, lifecycle machines, caches, service registries, message-group registries and thread managers, then mutates one of each category on node-0 and finds nodes 1 to 4 unchanged. Gates: node, bootstrap and transport suites 7788 with one failure, fresh-join-via-non-seed-node, which is pre-existing flaky at 1 in 6 on HEAD as well as 2 in 6 here; strict substrate zero seams and proof-eligible; same-process three runs and two fresh processes byte-identical, and still exactly the sealed legacy oracle at 391 a4c6ec504df54558; host blocks 0, 50, 200 and 500 ms identical; zero post-return production effects and the next generation identical.

A2a production half landed: MessageRouterSetup.create takes an optional routerFactory whose default constructs today's MessageRouter with byte-identical options. Every semantic step stays where it was - service-node resolution, node-address resolution through the runtime's own NodeService and cache, the bulk-channel registry, initialize with or without a server, local-versus-remote routing and admission all remain MessageRouterSetup's and MessageRouter's. The factory receives the same option bag production builds and returns the router object; it decides nothing about addresses, identity or policy. Transport and bootstrap suites 6397 with only the pre-existing fresh-join flake.

The physical transport boundary is narrower and lower than the deliver() path suggests, which changes what the simulator half of A2a has to build. MessageRouter.deliver resolves the target node, applies pressure and routing policy and then reaches resolveDeliveryOutcome; the actual bytes leave at connection.ws.send(JSON.stringify(message)) in message-router-delivery-behaviors.js, against a WebSocket-like object held in the router's connection registry. So the deterministic environment is NOT a deliver() override or a router subclass - it is a ws-compatible endpoint backed by VirtualNetwork, plus connection establishment, so the real router keeps every routing decision and every same-node call still crosses the production boundary. That is the correct shape for the no-same-node-shortcut rule, and it is also the honest size of the remaining work: connection establishment includes the IDENTIFY handshake, the connection registry and reconnect suppression, none of which the formation simulator has needed until now. The A2a witness - two isolated runtimes, real MessageRouterSetup on each, delivery traversing VirtualNetwork both ways, address resolution from each node's own cache, and a mutation replacing the environment with a direct endpoint call - depends on that adapter and is not yet written.

A2a simulator half: the in-process physical transport is now injectable, and the simulator supplies a VirtualNetwork-backed implementation.

Production seam (default is today's behavior, unchanged): src/transport/in-process-connection-environment.js owns two facts that were previously hard-wired physics - the endpoint registry (the process-global INPROC.serversByPort) and the frame transport (createInProcWebSocketPair, microtask delivery). MessageRouter resolves it once in its constructor; startInProcessServer registers/releases through it; establishInProcessConnection looks an endpoint up through it and asks it for the socket pair, passing the dial context {portKey, address, localNodeId, remoteNodeId}. INPROC and createInProcWebSocketPair are no longer imported by either lifecycle module. 1500 transport tests pass unchanged.

Simulator half: test/distributed/harness/virtual-connection-environment.js. Its registry is scenario-local, so two scenarios in one process cannot dial each other's nodes and the process-global registry gains nothing. Its sockets are interface-compatible with InProcWebSocket (readyState, send, close, terminate, message/close/error) but send() enqueues the frame on the VirtualNetwork as an ordinary message event, so every frame - IDENTIFY included - consumes the link's virtual delay. A close travels the same way, behind anything already in flight, so a FIN can never overtake a frame sent before it. There is no same-node shortcut: a link between two runtimes co-hosted on one node is still a link and its frames are recorded from the node to itself. The physical open is immediate, because a dial is a local process operation.

What it does not model, deliberately: handshake latency, backpressure, fragmentation, half-open sockets, or any second copy of the link semantics the VirtualNetwork already owns.

The four A2a witnesses hold against real MessageRouters, and the two red mutations invert the one observation all three read.

Witness 1 (real identification over VirtualNetwork). The dialing end holds an open socket the instant connectToNode resolves, and the far end knows nothing: routerB.nodeConnections has no node-a, and network.now() is still 0. After the network delivers, the peer is known, virtual time has advanced past the link delay, and the frames that did it are link frames. Loopback self-connections identify over the link too, node-to-itself.

Witness 2 (admission still authoritative). With externalAdmissionEnabled false on node-b, a DELIVERED IDENTIFY is refused - node-a is absent while node-b's own self-connection is admitted exactly as before. Reopening the gate and re-dialing admits the same peer across the same environment, so the refusal was a decision and not a broken link.

Witness 3 (real service delivery with ACK). routerA.deliver('node-b/partition/p1', ...) runs the handler on the remote router, returns acknowledged=true and deliveryState=delivered, and request and acknowledgement are separate link frames that consumed virtual time.

Witness 4 (runtime-local address authority). Two scenarios claim the SAME ports simultaneously - impossible under the process global, which would be EADDRINUSE - each resolves its own node-b, a dial inside one never reaches the other, the sibling network's clock never moves, and INPROC.serversByPort gains nothing.

Red mutations. Both are read through the same observation function witness 1 reads, so what they falsify is witness 1 itself. (a) socket send() emitting on the peer directly, the way the process-global transport does: the peer is identified with no frame on the link and no virtual time consumed. (b) the environment rekeying the far end's connection table at dial time: the peer is admitted before its IDENTIFY was delivered. In both cases atDial.peerKnown - the whole discriminator between a real link and a host callback - inverts from false to true.

Frontier recorded, not closed: the MessageRouter owner still holds 35 ambient Date.now() reads across 11 files (reconnect behaviors 8, delivery behaviors 6, outbound delivery registry 5, and so on). A2a does not compose the router into the guarded runner, so the strict guard is not yet exercised against them; closing them is its own owner.

Three ratchets were red before this slice, and two of them were this branch's own debt rather than inherited.

Unused exports: origin/main is exactly at baseline (1438/1438); the branch's committed HEAD was 1449. The eleven are all branch-introduced internal symbols with no consumer anywhere - MAX_DRAIN_ROUNDS and NOT_IDLE_ERROR (raft task tracker), PRIORITY_RECOVERY_PLANNING_READ_MODE, GAP_THRESHOLD_MS, CALIBRATION_FILE, NondeterministicOwnerSeam, unguardedHarnessWork, FORMATION_OWNER, OBSERVATION_KIND, planningGateObservation, NOT_REACHED_ERROR. De-exported; four of them (the read-mode enum, unguardedHarnessWork, planningGateObservation and the observation-kind enum it used) turned out to be dead code and were deleted rather than hidden. My own four new exports were de-exported the same way, so the slice is ratchet-neutral: 1438/1438.

Complexity: 1821 against a 1820 baseline. The single new violation was NodeService.initialize crossing 12 to 13 on the A1a thread-manager fallback. Extracted resolveNodeServiceThreadManager next to the existing resolveNodeServiceClock, which is the file's own idiom; back to 1820/1820. No baseline was raised.

Duplication: 58/57 clone groups in src+scripts and 794/793 in test, both clean on origin/main. The src group was the two quest probes I wrote in earlier slices - formation-sim-attribution-isolation.js and formation-sim-production-time-authority.js were byte-identical apart from the witness path and one noun - now one runWitnessTapProbe owner in scripts/checks/witness-tap-probe.js, and a probe that measures nothing itself is exactly the property that owner protects. The test group was heldPromise + isPending duplicated between the reconcile-queue current-work witness and the gateway owner-completion witness; extracted to test/helpers/promise-settlement.js and adopted by the readiness-planning consistency witness too. Both back to baseline.

One copy was deliberately left alone: raft-protocol-task-tracker.test.js has an isPending whose race handles only fulfilment, so adopting the shared one would have quietly changed what that witness reports for a rejected promise. It was not part of the new clone group and is not new debt.

Separately, pre-existing and NOT this branch's: test/raft/liferaft-formation-attribution-interaction.test.js fails five subtests identically on origin/main, on 5da0d7348 and on HEAD. Its mutation witness asserts that reverting the protocol mapping drives raft_protocol durationUs to 0, and it now measures 10, 9 and 7 microseconds instead. That is a mutation witness that no longer falsifies, in the raft attribution owner, on main. Recorded, not repaired here.

A2a closed against its gates, with the branch's ratchet debt paid on the way.

Suites: transport 1500/1500; transport + bootstrap + control-plane + workflow + raft + scripts + simulation + node is 20958 tests with no failure this branch introduced. The same wide batch at committed HEAD fails a superset of what it fails here, and one of HEAD's reds - 'producer serializes the exact canonical emitted module closure', red on origin/main too - goes green here because regenerating the three shard classification seals for the new witness files fixed the census the producer reads. The residual reds are all reproduced at HEAD or on main: the fresh-join non-seed flake, Property 11 and the MOVE_REPLICA sweep (both green in isolation, batch interference), the raft attribution mutation witness, and run-test-files plus the two runner-cap witnesses in test/scripts.

Static gate: green end to end. Complexity 1820/1820, cognitive at baseline, duplication 57/57 and 793/793, unused exports 1438/1438, shards and impact contracts exit 0, lint clean over src, test and scripts.

Determinism unchanged: two runs of one seed hash identical, and the reproduction probe still reports the same 3 unmet predicates it reported before this slice (seed gap, five-node lease/backoff, control_plane_pressure). Those are what B through G are for; nothing here was expected to move them.

Not done here, and deliberately: A2a composes no production bootstrap phase. The seam and its simulator implementation exist and are witnessed, but no simulator scenario has been cut over to them yet. That is A2b (real BootstrapService.phaseInfrastructure on node-0, with the dual-owner falsifier) and A2c (createProductionBootstrapSimNode).

A2b: node-0's phase-one infrastructure is composed by a real BootstrapService, and the real phase-one path is now inside the strict proof cone.

The harness supplies environment and nothing else: an isolated NodeService (uninitialised), an isolated thread manager, a VirtualNetwork, networkTimeSource(node-0), the A2a VirtualConnectionEnvironment and a routerFactory that builds the router inside it. createProductionBootstrapPhaseOneHost composes no MessageRouter, SystemTableCache, CDCIntegrationService, RebalanceCoordinator, ControlPlaneReadinessService, TablePolicyService, PartitionService or MessageGroupService; it refuses any of them as an argument.

One environmental dependency was missing and is now wired: BootstrapService takes an optional routerFactory and threads it to SeedInfrastructurePhase and on to MessageRouterSetup.create. Production passes none and the setup owner constructs today's MessageRouter.

The real SeedInfrastructurePhase.phaseInfrastructure() runs inside generation + executionNodeId=node-0. It was never called outside the node frame: A2b's whole point is that this path is measured where production runs.

What the phase produced, all of it production's: the supplied runtime stayed the node authority and holds node-0's identity; bootstrap.messageRouter exists and is bootstrap.transport, built by MessageRouterSetup through the factory exactly once with node-0's identity, address and port; serviceLifecycleManager and serviceReconciler exist and the phase's initial reconciliation completed with reason bootstrap_infrastructure_ready and zero failures. Desired state is empty - messageGroupServices, partitionServices, messageGroupReplicas, partitionReplicas all zero, and the reconciler took no action because none was desired - and cdcIntegrationService, rebalanceCoordinator and tablePolicyService are still null.

The self-connection is production's own. The witness never dials: the router does, from initialize(). The endpoint that answers the dial is the phase's own router in the scenario-local registry, the link is the only one, and the IDENTIFY is a frame on it. The phase does NOT wait for identification - the socket is open, the frame is in flight, and the inbound half carries no peer identity - so the discriminator is that field: null before delivery, node-0 after, established by real inbound IDENTIFY handling over the VirtualNetwork, with link time consumed and node-0 dialling itself still crossing the network.

Strict mode named five clock owners on the real phase-one path, in first-refusal order. Each was repaired at its semantic owner; no time was put into the VirtualConnectionEnvironment to make a refusal disappear, and no production default changed.

1. NodeService.initialize, on its own startTime. The runtime already had a  initialize seam but nothing could reach it, because the phase initialises the runtime itself. NodeService now takes the runtime's clock at construction (timeSource, with the explicit  option still winning), exposes it as getTimeSource(), and reads it for every node-local stamp - startTime, service startedAt, stoppedAt and lastHealthCheck were still on Date.now.

2. NodeLifecycleStateMachine, stamping this node's transitions. It has always had a  seam; nothing threaded the runtime's answer in, so it fell back to the host. One line.

3. The MessageRouter owner. This is the frontier the design predicted, and it took ONE router TimeSource rather than separate clocks: 35 Date.now reads and 27 timers across eleven files now read this.timeSource / router.timeSource. Connection age, queue wait, ping liveness, reconnect due-times, quarantine windows and the shutdown drain are statements about one node's time and now come from one source. The default is a RealTimeSource, so production is unchanged - which is exactly why strict refused a RealTimeSource.now() read and forced the simulator to supply the node's clock rather than silently accepting the host's.

4. The bulk-transfer channel registry, whose token bucket read the host clock at construction. It already accepted ; MessageRouterSetup now passes the router's, so the registry a router owns reads that router's clock.

5. ServiceReconciler, arming its cadence on the host. It gained resolveTimeSource(options) and now reads it for the interval and every cycle timing; StartupServiceLifecycleOwner passes the node's, through a getTimeSource delegate on SeedInfrastructurePhase.

Two production repairs fell out of the same path. MessageRouter.startPingInterval called unref() unguarded, alone among that owner's timers - a handle from a non-host time source has no event loop to release; it is now guarded like its siblings. And NodeService's lazily created system-table cache read Date.now for a debug identity and had no clock at all: it now reads the node's clock and is named after the node, which is unique wherever the timestamp was and has no semantic consumer.

Separately, A2b exposed a VirtualNetwork defect that the legacy scenario never reached: enqueue() pushes a COPY of the event, so an adapter timer's record held a reference that was never the queued object and cancelling it removed nothing. A cancelled timer declined to fire but stayed pending - answering pendingEventCount() and peekNextEventInstant(), the two readings a quiescence driver uses - and firing it still stamped the node's clock and wrote a FIRED record. Nothing in the legacy scenario cancels a timer before it fires, which is why it was latent; a composed production node does, every time a router or reconciler shuts down. Repaired, with a directed witness that goes red against the old enqueue. The seed-7 report is byte-identical before and after, so the legacy substrate never depended on it.

Correction to the previous finding: three backticked words were eaten by the shell before they reached the log. The seams named are NodeService's explicit initialize-time clock option (now), the lifecycle state machine's own clock option (now), and the bulk-transfer registry's clock option (now). No other text was affected.

A2b gates.

Composition witness: 10 of 10 green, including the two negatives. A1 isolation witnesses, the A2a connection-environment witnesses 6 of 6, and the time-authority witnesses all green.

Strict: violations 0, substitutions 0, mode strict, proofEligible true, across the whole phase including delivery of the self IDENTIFY.

Determinism: same-process exact (two composed runs produce identical transcripts and end at the same instant), fresh-process exact (a child process reproduces the transcript and the final instant), host-block invariant (200k iterations of synchronous burn between settlement turns changes nothing), post-seal zero effects (nothing pending after teardown, no enqueue after the seal).

Teardown follows production ownership: the phase's lifecycle owners stop, then the router shuts down and releases its own endpoint through the environment's release operation, then the runtime shuts down. The witness clears no connection table, no handler map, no desired-state map and no endpoint registry.

Legacy substrate untouched: the seed-7 report is byte-identical to the one committed HEAD produces, sha256 0517da2b7f26e1e58ca8d1bc22ffad0878a05a780d4da9b5ad4853db9a4e21ef, before and after the VirtualNetwork cancellation repair. The reproduction probe still reports the same three unmet predicates - seed gap, five-node lease and backoff, control_plane_pressure - with two runs of one seed hashing identical. No new production-composed oracle was captured.

Ratchets: the router clock and cache-ownership work pushed NodeService from 794 to 841 lines, over the 800 threshold. Repaired by extraction rather than a raised baseline: the runtime's thread manager, clock and node-local cache moved to node-runtime-local-authorities.js, and the node statistics snapshot to the statistics sampler that already owned the host reading. Back to 27/27.

Two test updates, both because a stub grew a contract rather than because an assertion moved. The CL-009 outbound-saturation stub router now carries a timeSource, since a router's queue stamps from the router's clock. The three shard classification files gained the new witness file.

Pre-existing and not A2b's: the LifeRaft attribution mutation witness, reproduced identically on origin/main and on older heads, stays recorded and unsuppressed. The fresh-join non-seed flake, Property 11, Property 7 and the Cluster.stop playback teardown all reproduce at committed HEAD or on main.

Transcript, two-layer host, and the small A2c composition witness.

The transcript is the simulation host's artifact. No production object emits into it; every entry is observation of a boundary production already has. The physical transport reports in LINK vocabulary only - an endpoint bound, a socket opened, a frame moved between two nodes - and never reads a payload, so deciding that a frame was an IDENTIFY stays at MessageRouter's own control boundary, where it is taken from the NODE_IDENTIFIED event the router already emits. Two ordinary assignments are observed with instance property descriptors rather than new production events: the lifecycle manager and reconciler the startup owner sets, and NodeService.initialize, so node_runtime_initialized lands where it happens instead of being inferred afterwards from the phase's return.

It is capture only. Recording never flushes a microtask, advances the network, awaits an owner, polls or sleeps. Incidental entropy is not filtered after capture: the contract admits exactly seq, virtualTimeMs, event, nodeId, peerNodeId, owner, phase and frameKind, and refuses anything else at record time, so router ids, connection ids and host timestamps were never fields. A semantic entry after the seal is refused as a failure rather than dropped.

The causal chain the transcript proves, on one node with a 1 ms link:

  seq 12 t=0  phase_infrastructure_completed
  seq 13 t=1  frame_delivered
  seq 14 t=1  identify_received
  seq 15 t=1  self_identity_bound

and, read at the moment the phase returned, the transcript ends at seq 12 with frame_enqueued present and frame_delivered absent. Production is left exactly as it is: phaseInfrastructure() returns with the self socket open and its IDENTIFY in flight. The host gained settleCausalConsequences(), which walks the existing closeCurrentInstant/advanceToNextInstant authority; it decides nothing about closure itself.

Two layers now. createProductionSimNodeEnvironment owns only what a node needs to exist - runtime, thread manager, network place, clock, endpoint, physical routerFactory, transcript observer - and composes nothing semantic. createProductionSeedSimHost mounts the real BootstrapService on one. No host takes a mode flag: the join path will mount a different production owner on the same environment, and A2c-3 states that structurally.

Determinism gates over the four artifacts, and the small A2c result.

Four artifacts are compared whole, never selected counters: the host transcript, the VirtualNetwork transcript, the strict report and the provenance snapshot, plus the transcript as it stood when the phase returned and again after causal closure. All six are exact across every axis on which the host may differ and the scenario may not - three same-process runs; three fresh plain-node processes compared against this process, which is the test runner, so that doubles as the node-versus-node-test gate; synchronous host burden of 0, 50k, 200k and 500k iterations injected as an owner-idle contract inside the existing closure authority rather than through a hook invented for it; and no host observer, an observer, and an observer capturing stacks.

Post-seal, checked over four observer checkpoints rather than one: the transcript did not grow, the scheduler received no new event, nothing is pending, no wall-clock resource is alive, and the only escaped host resource is a single inert PROMISE reaction. Any non-Promise escape would be a failure.

A2c collapsed as expected. Five environments coexist on one scheduler with distinct runtimes, thread managers, clocks and identities, sharing one network, one physical transport and one transcript, and five clocks read one instant while all five nodes run. An environment composes nothing: no runtime initialised, no cache built by merely existing, transcript length zero. Mounting the seed on node-0 leaves node-1 through node-4 uninitialised, cacheless, routerless and endpointless, the single bound endpoint belongs to the seed, and every semantic boundary in the transcript names node-0 alone. A2c needed no new implementation - A1, A2a and A2b had already earned it - so it is a composition witness rather than a slice.

Gates: composition witness 8 of 8, determinism 5 of 5, five-node composition 3 of 3, virtual-network 45 of 45, and the A1/A2a/time-authority witnesses unchanged. Legacy substrate still byte-identical at sha256 0517da2b7f26e1e58ca8d1bc22ffad0878a05a780d4da9b5ad4853db9a4e21ef and the reproduction probe still reports the same three unmet predicates. Three new exports that nothing imports were de-exported rather than baselined.

Not touched: the pre-existing LifeRaft attribution mutation witness.

Verification cost baseline, 2026-09-16, recorded as a measurement rather than an aside.

Measured on this machine during the A2b and transcript slices:

  focused witness file                 1-3 s
  seed-7 simulator run                 ~2 s
  formation-sim-reproduces probe       ~5 s
  wide test sweep, ~32k tests          7-10 min
  npm run test:static, full gate       6-9 min
  pre-commit hook on one commit        8-12 min, of which ~2 min is the
                                       import-graph inventory regeneration

The shape matters more than the numbers: the simulator and its witnesses are
fast, and essentially all elapsed time is verification infrastructure. Two
consequences for how slices are run. During development, iterate on focused
witnesses and defer the expensive path until the implementation is coherent.
And later harness work should be able to show that verification SCHEDULING
improved against this baseline without weakening any proof - fewer minutes for

B: node-0 runs the real phaseMessageGroups(), and three production-owned MessageGroupService runtimes exist on it.

The chain, read straight off the host transcript at one node with a 1 ms link:

  t=1    message_group_replica_declared  mg-1-r1, r2, r3
  t=1    message_group_replica_created / started / reconciler_action_executed  r1
  t=51   the same three for r2

  t=101  message_group_election_deferred  r1, r2, r3
  t=101  phase_message_groups_completed

Every declaration precedes every creation, so desired state is complete before the first runtime is built - the phase queues and the reconciler acts, rather than creating inline. Each action is create_start_replica, owned by ServiceReconciler. Three real MessageGroupService instances exist, keyed by the declared replica ids, each with groupId mg-1, nodeId node-0, deferElection true, the whole group as peers, and every peer address on node-0. Each reads the runtime's own cache and the runtime's own clock, not a process singleton's. partitionServices and partitionReplicas are still empty: C is a separate slice.

The stagger is the interesting fact. The 50 ms replica stagger is now paced on the NODE's clock, so the three creations land exactly one stagger apart in VIRTUAL time and the phase itself cannot return until virtual time has advanced. Phase one never blocked on virtual time; phase two does. The host gained driveUntilSettled, which runs the existing closure authority while a phase is in flight and advances only until the phase settles - so 'the phase returned' and 'its consequences settled' stay separate facts even for a phase that waits.

Deferred election is asserted as scheduling rather than as a flag: with three replicas alive, no timer is armed anywhere near a consensus cadence. The only two armed are phase one's, at 30 s and an hour.

B's first-refusal sequence: six owners, each repaired where it belongs.

1. ServiceLifecycleManager had no clock. Its five duration and timestamp sites now read one injected source, threaded from the node runtime through StartupServiceLifecycleOwner beside the reconciler's.

2. The bootstrap sleep - replica staggering - waited on the host loop. It is node-local pacing, so it waits on the node's clock. This is what turns the stagger into virtual time.

3. ServiceReconciler took one real event-loop turn per action with setImmediate. The turn belongs to the node it acts for, so it is now a zero-delay timer on that node's clock: the same macrotask boundary, on the substrate that owns the node's scheduling.

4. MessageGroupService reached for NodeService.getInstance() for its node-local cache. That is the A1 collapse at a new owner: with several runtimes in a process every replica would read one node's cache as its own. It now takes the runtime, defaulting to the singleton.

5. Its HLC clock read the host. HLCClockService already had the seam; nothing threaded the replica's clock into it.

6. Consensus timers armed on liferaft's own tick-tock. RaftGroup now forwards a timeSource when the hosting node owns one, and leaves liferaft alone when it does not.

One repair was WRONG the first time and the corpus caught it. The peer-reconciliation coalescing hop also used setImmediate, and I replaced it with a zero-delay timer unconditionally. setImmediate and setTimeout(0) are DIFFERENT event-loop phases, so that changed production's ordering rather than its substrate, and two message-group reconciliation witnesses went red. The hop now takes the node's clock only when the node owns one and keeps setImmediate otherwise - which is the rule the liferaft seam already followed, applied consistently.

One deliberate non-repair: raft-replica-base-runtime-helpers.js has the same consensus-timer seam for PARTITION replicas. B does not reach it, so it is left alone. It is C's, and recorded here rather than fixed opportunistically.

Also recorded, not repaired: BootstrapService.shutdown takes a host setImmediate hop. Teardown is not part of B's chain and the composed host does not reach it.

And one latent harness defect of my own, found by B: settleCausalConsequences treated its horizon as an ABSOLUTE instant rather than as how much further the scenario may run, so a phase that had already consumed virtual time got no room for its consequences. Phase one never noticed because it ended at t=1; phase two ends at t=101. Fixed.
